phonemes.desc: The canonical restored form Makemake, built on the reduplicated Polynesian element make — in Hawaiian the exact cognate makemake means 'to want, to desire'; the Rapa Nui lexicon glosses the god's name 'to see, to know'.

pronunciation.approximation: Say 'makemake' with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration 'Makemake'.

domains.title: Makemake
domains.subtitle: Creator
domains.lead: Makemake is the creator god of Rapa Nui — Easter Island: father of fertility, lord of the seabirds, and the hidden face behind the island's birdman cult. His carved eyes watch from the stone village of Orongo, where each spring a contest chose the tangata manu, the man who bore the god's sign for a year.

cards.name: Tangata Manu
cards.desc: The birdman of the Orongo contest — the year's chosen lord, raised by Makemake's sign: the first sooty-tern egg brought unbroken from Motu Nui.

cards.name: Creator of Rapa Nui
cards.desc: Head of the island's recorded pantheon: maker of humankind, father of fertility, lord of the manu, the birds on which the island's life depended.

cards.name: Orongo
cards.desc: The stone village on the rim of the Rano Kau crater, where hundreds of petroglyphs carry Makemake's enormous staring face.

cards.name: Tapati Rapa Nui
cards.desc: The island's annual festival, where the birdman legend is staged again — the tradition's living return after the nineteenth-century silence.

symbols.name: The sooty tern's egg
symbols.meaning: The unbroken egg carried from Motu Nui by the swimmer: Makemake's annual sign, the seed of the birdman's year of sacred rule.

symbols.name: The wide-eyed face
symbols.meaning: Makemake's carved visage at Orongo, eyes hugely enlarged: the god as watcher — seeing and knowing everything that happens below, the lexicon's gloss made stone.

symbols.name: Frigatebird (manu)
symbols.meaning: The great sea-bird of the contest islets; manu, 'bird', is the root of tangata manu, the birdman himself, and of the god's lordship over the flocks.

symbols.name: Rano Kau crater
symbols.meaning: The great volcanic bowl above Orongo whose rim is the ceremonial stage of the birdman cult — the island's sacred theater, open to the sea.

symbols.name: Aku aku
symbols.meaning: The guardian spirits of the caves in the recorded lore — attendants of Makemake's hidden realm, keepers of what the island buried.

mythology.lead: Makemake is the creator god of Rapa Nui (Easter Island): father of fertility, lord of the seabirds, and the hidden face behind the island's birdman cult. The sources are late — the tradition was recorded in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, after the population's collapse — and they must be read as the memory of a wounded tradition.

myths.title: The Creator in the Chants
myths.text: When the first ethnographers asked the islanders who made the world, the answer was Makemake. Alfred Métraux, working on Rapa Nui in 1934–35, recorded chants in which Makemake appears at the beginning of things as the great god, the maker of humankind, attended by the aku aku, the guardian spirits of the caves; Katherine Routledge heard related accounts during the Mana expedition of 1914–15. The surviving material is fragmentary — Peruvian slave raids and smallpox had shattered the population in the 1860s, carrying off the initiated experts, and much of the theology survived in the mouths of a handful of elders. In the recorded lore Makemake stands at the head of the pantheon, paired with the sea-god Tangaroa. What can be said with confidence is this: on the most isolated inhabited island on earth, creation was not a distant cosmic event but a local one, governed by a god whose staring face was carved into the living stone of the island itself.

myths.title: The Birdman Contest
myths.text: Each spring the men of Rapa Nui gathered at Orongo, the stone village on the rim of the Rano Kau crater, to compete for the title of tangata manu — the birdman. Swimmers called hopu descended the sea cliffs and crossed shark-filled water to the islet of Motu Nui, there to await the sooty tern's first egg of the season. The sponsor whose hopu returned first with an unbroken egg won: he was shaved, painted red and black, given the egg to wear against his body, and seated for a year in sacred seclusion as Makemake's chosen — the year's lord of fertility, whose fortune was read in the fortunes of land and sea. Métraux reconstructed the full ritual cycle from informants' testimony, and Routledge saw the last performances in 1914. The contest means that on an island without kingship, legitimacy came not from conquest but from a god-given sign: the birdman's egg was the island's crown, and Makemake alone conferred it.

myths.title: The Eyes of Orongo
myths.text: The village of Orongo is itself Makemake's great icon. Its flat lava slabs are covered with petroglyphs — birdmen with human faces and birds' bodies, frigatebirds, Komari fertility symbols, and above all the staring face of Makemake himself, the eyes hugely enlarged, peering from the rock beside the contest grounds. Georgia Lee's survey, The Rock Art of Easter Island (1992), catalogued some twelve hundred designs and showed the wide-eyed faces clustered at the very village where the tangata manu contest was held: the god carved as witness. Métraux had already recorded that the islanders named these faces as Makemake's. The image means that knowledge is sight — the lexicon's gloss of the name, 'to see, to know', is literally carved at Orongo, where the god's whole function is to watch, and where being seen by Makemake is the entire power of the ceremony.

myths.title: The Silence and the Return
myths.text: The cult did not survive contact intact. Peruvian slavers carried off around a thousand islanders in 1862–63, including the last initiated experts; smallpox followed; by 1868 the survivors stood for mass baptism. Métraux heard the birdman cycle from men who had never seen it performed, and Routledge found Orongo already standing empty, its sacred houses abandoned. Yet the name never died. In the later twentieth century the Tapati Rapa Nui festival began staging the birdman legend again — canoe races, body-painting, and the choosing of a festival queen — and the tangata manu story became the emblem of the islanders' revived identity. In 2008 the astronomers who found the bright dwarf planet beyond Pluto gave it Makemake's name. The history means that a god once reduced to a stone face watched over the slow return of the people who had made him: the watcher outlasted the silence.

lore.syncretism: Makemake had no classical syncretism — there was no neighboring pantheon on the loneliest island in the world. His transformation came with catastrophe: after the Peruvian slave raids and epidemics of the 1860s, the survivors embraced Catholicism, and the creator god was absorbed into the image of the Christian God or quietly retired to the petroglyphs. Comparison with other Polynesian traditions remains the useful lens: Tahiti's Ta'aroa and the wide Tangaroa-complex of the eastern Pacific give the intellectual frame for understanding how a high creator-god sits above a crowd of specialist spirits and ancestor-deities. In the modern world the identification has run in reverse — the dwarf planet Makemake, named in 2008 after the Easter Island god, has carried the name of a Polynesian creator into every astronomy textbook, a rare case of a colonial-era suppressed deity colonizing the heavens.
lore.culturalLegacy: The birdman's egg became the island's flag: the Tapati Rapa Nui festival, held each February, stages canoe races and dance competitions in which the old birdman legend is the centerpiece, and the winner's crown echoes the tangata manu's year of rule. Orongo, restored as a ceremonial village, anchors the UNESCO-listed Rapa Nui National Park. In 2008 the International Astronomical Union named the dwarf planet Makemake — one of the largest objects in the Kuiper belt — after the god, explicitly honoring Easter Island's cultural heritage. Meanwhile the Rapa Nui language, once nearly extinct, is taught again in island schools, and with it the old names return to living mouths. A tradition recorded from the last survivors of a catastrophe has become the founding charter of a cultural renaissance.
lore.extendedMeditation: Makemake is the god of the watching face: on an island of 165 square kilometers, where every horizon ends in ocean, creation was a matter of sight — the god who sees, the god who knows. His cult turned that metaphysics into sport: each year the whole society wagered its fertility on who could first see, and bring back, a single egg. The birdman contest is among the most beautiful institutions in the ethnographic record — an election without ballots, a kingship without war, legitimacy conferred by a seabird's arithmetic. And the lesson of the silence matters as much as the contest: traditions recorded from the last elders, like the chants Métraux wrote down in 1934, are not museum pieces but threads — cut, they take whole cosmologies with them. Makemake's staring eyes at Orongo are a reminder that being watched is the oldest form of being known.
lore.archaeology: The material evidence is concentrated at Orongo, the ceremonial village on the Rano Kau crater rim: some fifty stone houses and over a thousand petroglyphs, including the wide-eyed Makemake faces and birdman figures documented by Routledge (1914–15) and catalogued by Georgia Lee (1992). Several carved slabs were removed to museums in the 1970s after weathering and vandalism; the village was consolidated under William Mulloy's restoration program. The islets of Motu Nui, Motu Iti and Motu Kao Kao below the cliffs preserve the contest's arena; Rano Raraku's quarry and the ahu platforms (notably Ahu Tongariki) form the wider sacred landscape. The Rapa Nui National Park has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995.
